title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
gist: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's blog post "We Must Pace the Frontier" calls for US-China cooperation to slow AI while simultaneously urging Washington to maximize its lead through chip-smuggling crackdowns and blocking model distillation, and Chinese officials, researchers and AI companies read that conditionality as a bad-faith deal. Beijing's Ministry of Foreign Affairs called it fearmongering, analysts say Chinese policymakers see US safety rhetoric as instrumental positioning ahead of IPOs, and a DeepSeek researcher publicly rejected letting Anthropic or OpenAI control AGI — all as preliminary US-China talks proceed ahead of Xi Jinping's planned Washington visit.

themes.theme: Silicon Valley's pivot from race to pacing

insights.claim: After years of arguing the US is locked in an AI arms race with China that it cannot afford to lose, the same Silicon Valley executives shifted within a week to arguing the two countries urgently need to cooperate to slow the race down.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: An abrupt narrative inversion by the same actors is a positioning tell: watch what policy asks accompany the safety rhetoric, not the rhetoric itself.
insights.locator: For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley

insights.claim: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post titled "We Must Pace the Frontier" that global pacing will require cooperation with China, which he described as the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: A frontier lab CEO conceding China holds the most advanced non-US capabilities reframes export-control debates around parity rather than containment.
insights.quote: Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities
insights.locator: “Global pacing will require cooperation with China

insights.claim: Amodei argued that a key part of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring democracies maintain as large a lead as possible over autocracies, urging the US to crack down on chip smuggling and prevent unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: The concrete asks are enforcement actions on semiconductors and distillation — the actionable policy surface for chip supply chains and open-weight model access.
insights.locator: Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy

insights.claim: The article calls Amodei's claim that weakening China's AI industry would give the US more leverage and make a future agreement more likely a heroic leap in logic that is left unexplained, noting he later admitted on television that he has no idea how to negotiate with China.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: The absence of a credible negotiation theory means the proposal functions mainly as a domestic policy ask, not a viable diplomatic track.
insights.quote: no idea how to negotiate with China
insights.locator: Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic

themes.theme: Why Beijing reads it as a bad deal

insights.claim: Chinese government bodies and AI companies are deeply skeptical of Amodei's proposal not because they reject AI risk but because they think they are being offered a bad deal, according to the article's central framing.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Reframing Chinese resistance as deal-terms rejection rather than risk denial identifies negotiable terms, which is where any real agreement would form.
insights.quote: They think they’re being offered a bad deal.
insights.locator: China’s government and AI companies have made it clear

insights.claim: Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under Barack Obama, says China's AI safety community is growing and shares many of the same concerns as American labs, with the gulf being over sequencing and status rather than substance.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: If the disagreement is procedural rather than substantive, a symmetric framing could unlock cooperation faster than most geopolitical risk models assume.
insights.quote: The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.
insights.locator: “The AI safety community in China is growing

insights.claim: Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, says Amodei's essay makes AI pacing conditional on increasing the US lead over China, which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Conditionality is the specific design flaw sinking the proposal; any workable framework must decouple safety terms from lead-maximization.
insights.quote: which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers
insights.locator: “His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional

insights.claim: Chinese officials, researchers and commentators resent being treated simultaneously as an essential governance partner and as a competitor that needs to be constrained, without disputing that AI poses risks.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: The dual-role contradiction is the structural obstacle to any US-led AI governance regime that also functions as an export-control regime.
insights.locator: The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators

insights.claim: Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, described the proposal at a Monday press conference as fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: An on-record MFA rejection sets the official ceiling for what Chinese negotiators can concede in near-term talks.
insights.locator: When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference

insights.claim: China's foreign ministry stressed the day after rejecting the proposal that the country puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI, signaling it will not trade growth for safety commitments.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Equal-emphasis language means Chinese compute and model buildout continues regardless of governance talks — no capex slowdown to trade on.
insights.quote: China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI
insights.locator: The next day, the ministry also stressed

themes.theme: Divergent risk models: CCP stability versus extinction

insights.claim: Unlike the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China's leaders are not primarily concerned about existential AI risks such as a rogue agent killing everyone on Earth; Beijing's prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party's grip on power.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Mismatched threat models mean US x-risk framing will keep failing; proposals framed around regime-stability risks are the ones Beijing can accept.
insights.locator: The mixed comments are reflective of another reason

insights.claim: Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security, says Beijing is skeptical that AGI is achievable and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity, and although it is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks the risk it worries about most is the threat AI poses to CCP rule.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
entities: Center for a New American Security
insights.so_what: Beijing's AGI skepticism implies it will not self-limit compute buildout on capability-timeline arguments alone.
insights.quote: Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.
insights.locator: “Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value

insights.claim: China's minister of state security Chen Yixin warned in a recent essay that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest and new military threats, spending far less time on the doomsday scenarios that preoccupy US frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: A security-ministry threat list points to where Chinese AI regulation will actually bite: content, cyber and espionage controls, not capability caps.
insights.locator: In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security

themes.theme: Safety rhetoric read as commercial positioning

insights.claim: Michelle Nie says Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies' calls for AI safety as instrumental, believing those companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down competitors that are primarily Chinese.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Explicitly links AI safety messaging to pre-IPO valuation management — a lens to apply to every frontier-lab safety announcement in the listing window.
insights.quote: They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.
insights.locator: “Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls

insights.claim: Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, argues that Amodei's missive may backfire because rhetoric about weakening China erodes the fragile trust diplomatic talks depend on.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Even within the AI safety community the proposal is seen as self-defeating, weakening the coalition Anthropic would need to convert it into policy.
insights.quote: Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously
insights.locator: Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei

insights.claim: China's AI industry has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models, and that industry shares the skepticism toward US safety appeals.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Open-weight, low-cost releases are both a commercial strategy and a political stance, and they structurally undercut any pacing regime built on closed frontier labs.
insights.locator: That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry

insights.claim: A DeepSeek researcher wrote in a widely shared essay that AI could push society toward one of two extremes — broadly available powerful AI that raises living standards, or a handful of tech companies controlling the most advanced systems and resources, making it harder for everyone else to catch up.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: The concentration-versus-diffusion framing is the ideological basis for continued Chinese open-weight releases, which caps pricing power for closed model providers.
insights.locator: In a widely shared essay published on Sunday

insights.claim: The DeepSeek engineer wrote that he does not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to make the most advanced intelligence available openly and inexpensively, and especially does not want Anthropic controlling the most advanced AI or AGI.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Named distrust of specific US labs by a leading Chinese lab's researcher signals continued aggressive open-weight releases as a competitive weapon.
insights.quote: I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.
insights.locator: “That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence

insights.claim: Preliminary US-China negotiations are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping's planned visit to Washington later this month to meet President Donald Trump.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: A dated summit gives a near-term catalyst window for any announced AI governance language, chip policy shift or tariff linkage.
insights.locator: Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway

insights.claim: Both governments have expressed worry about the same specific issues — cybersecurity threats, misuse of powerful models, and increasingly capable AI systems behaving in unexpected ways — defining the narrow surface where agreement is plausible.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Any deliverable from the summit will most likely be scoped to cyber and misuse, not compute or capability limits.
insights.locator: There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful

insights.claim: Michelle Nie says what might move the needle most is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments, making verification mechanisms rather than pledges the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Louise Matsakis
insights.so_what: Verification infrastructure — chip tracking, compute attestation, audit regimes — is the concrete build-out any real deal would require.
insights.quote: designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments
insights.locator: “There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides
